q: The easiest way to improve classroom behavior is one few teachers ever consider.
It doesn’t entail making drastic changes. It doesn’t entail extra planning or specialized training.
Walk into any polite classroom anywhere in the world and there you will find well-behaved students.
These three alone will change the tone of your classroom, inspire more profound acts of kindness, and result in better overall classroom behavior.
But you must be the leader, the chief role model, the pillar of politeness. Every day. Sarcasm, impatience, and grouchiness will undo any good vibrations you’ve created.
Teaching politeness is a simple little thing. Easily disregarded, quickly forgotten, and too 1950s for today’s educational complexities.

q: Each of them are excellent teachers, and I'd argue that their excellence is something separate from personality or teaching style.

The thing about great teachers is that they are professionally dissatisfied with their shortcomings, their weaknesses, their mistakes, their inability to overcome present obstacles. And yet, because they believe that they can change and improve (in short, they have Carol Dweck's famous growth mindset), this dissatisfaction acts as a pleasant fuel that drives them to exert themselves toward improvement with every working hour.

Great teachers are just like these ultra-runners. They realize that a teaching career is a long path, and greatest are the rewards for those who stick to the work until they've put in enough deliberate practice to cross into excellence.

Their students are engaged in some form of thinking, reading, writing, or speaking from bell-to-bell; when kids are listening to the teacher, it's for a focused, organized message or lesson — not an endless, time-consuming string of self-indulgent anecdotes.

This intimacy with failure is only possible because these teachers have intentionally sought to detach their sense of self-worth from how well they're performing at work. Doing this is, as they say, “an inside job,” but it's critical if one wants to be able to analyze one's practice as objectively as possible.

They seek to rid themselves of self-righteousness or arrogance because they know, either instinctively or because the research supports it, that individual teachers do not create whole system change — groups of teachers do.
I'll end with the first mindset: remember that we're never finished working on improving as teachers, and we're never finished letting our work as teachers improve us. This work is a refining fire.

t: Why You Should Never Use Reflection Forms
q: Reflection forms have been around forever. And at first glance, they appear to be a good idea.
Most students see reflection forms as just another consequence, a hoop to jump through with the least amount of hassle. So with little thought, they’ll scribble down what they think you want to hear.
Reflection forms take students away from their academic responsibilities. They give them a free pass not to do their work or pay attention.
Because self-reflection can never be forced. It has to happen naturally. And it will as long as you step aside and allow your classroom management plan to do its job.

As soon as you tell them what to think or how to feel, as soon as you begin questioning or forcing assurances, as soon as you hand them a reflection form to fill out . . . You interfere with true self-reflection.
True self-reflection is the byproduct of well-defined rules and consequences, every-single-time consistency, and a teacher that students trust.
x: Interfering with the process—by questioning, demanding assurances, or requiring a written form—triggers defensiveness and resentment instead of genuine reflection.

t: An Example of Deliberate Practice from my Actual Life
q: And yet, this personal character growth is not truly selfish, either — not if our aim is to help our students leverage these strengths toward their long-term growth. Heck, it's not even optional because one of the best ways to help our students develop character in themselves is if we show them with our lives that this work is worth doing.

This doesn't mean coming up with a whole lesson plan — character strengths instruction should not derail curricula. Instead, just look for the opportunity in the week to share with your students an example of character strength work in your own life.

Externally, running a blog seems simple to many people I talk to. But over the past three years, I've put at least a thousand hours into figuring out blogging. That might sound like a lot, but it averages out to a little less than an hour a day.

So that's what deliberate practice is like in blogging: it seems complex on the outside, but mostly it's just very boring and repetitive. With every week, I pick up a few more tricks, a few more tweaks, a few more troubleshooting workarounds to problems I've not yet been able to solve.

And those things, my friends, are only possible through the use of deliberate practice. It matters not what your dream is: deliberate practice — boring, un-sexy, lame deliberate practice — is what dreams are made of.

I was driven by a desire to not just think about sharing interesting work and meeting interesting people, but to actually do those things. So I did (and do) the work, bit by bit, in the little snatches of time that I make, and the cumulative results of all those little bits of boring work over the past three years have been life-changing.

q: Humility calls us to assume that the parent or guardian we are working with at any given time loves the kid more than we'll ever be able to. It calls us to assume that the parent, therefore, wants that child's long-term flourishing infinitely more than we ever can.
It's not a silver bullet, mind you, but a humble attitude disarms people and makes them believe in their gut that you're on their team because, in humility, you realize that you are.

You'll know you have communicated when, after a conversation, both parties know what they need to do or they feel better or both. You'll know you haven't communicated when, after a conversation, nothing has changed.

If I encounter an angry or offensive parent and my sense of self-worth is attached to how things go, then I'm going to fight or run to protect myself. Yet if I enter the same situation with professional detachment, I'm able to analyze it like one would a puzzle and determine how to best remedy things.
This enables action and disables the life-draining, I'm-a-victim mentality that I see killing far too many teachers. Folks, we're not victims. We're professionals.

If a parent insults you, it's generally not at all about you. It's about their own issues, their own idolatries, their own warped psyches. We'll know we've nailed this when we continue to wholeheartedly seek to serve them and their child even when they treat us horribly.
But when we leave that school building for the day, it's not as a failure. We don't haul home a load of self-recrimination. Why? Because we are not only teachers — we are people.

t: How Humility Makes Us Better, Saner Teachers
q: The pursuit of humility, once we properly understand the term, yields better relationships and faster growth. With that said, it makes great sense that we dig into humility in our continuing pursuit of better, saner teaching.

Most folks don't think they are proud because they liken pride to arrogance. When we conceive of pride as arrogance, we miss out because pride becomes something we can check off of our list, saying, “Oh, well, I don't think I'm awesome, so I'm not proud.” (Which is a bit arrogant, actually.)
It's common in American culture to misconstrue humility into an attitude of inadequacy. A person with false humility will think frequently about themselves and their shortcomings.

We should expect to experience disrespect in our jobs — people are complicated. We should expect disruptions to our plans, like fire drills and traffic jams. These are natural consequences of us not being omnipotent.
Perfectionism is bad for you because it makes impossible demands. Every lesson of every day can't go perfectly. Seek excellence while holding reasonable expectations.
I've never experienced a relational problem that I didn't play some role in creating. We always own at least a part of the responsibility in our relationship problems.

Essentially, Ellis attributes our stress not to external circumstances, but to what we believe about how external circumstances should be. For example, we get angry about traffic jams because we believe traffic jams shouldn't happen. But in reality, traffic jams totally happen all the time.
x: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that humility, properly understood, makes teachers both better at their work and saner, reducing the stress and frustration that feed burnout.
Stuart's key reframe is that pride means self-obsession rather than arrogance, so no one can claim to be free of it.

His first move is definitional: pride is not arrogance but self-obsession, which means false humility (deflecting compliments, dwelling on one's inadequacy) is itself pride, and true humility is self-forgetfulness.

True humility is defined as self-forgetfulness, operationalised in four aims including 'defy perfectionism' by seeking excellence with reasonable expectations.
For relational friction he prescribes asking how you contributed to the tension, on the premise that we always own part of our relationship problems.
Drawing on Albert Ellis, he locates teacher frustration in beliefs about how circumstances should be, so a humble teacher manages unrealistic expectations and grows faster.

q: Inconsistency is the number one reason students continue to break the same rules again and again.
Questioning, lecturing, forcing assurances, and the like is too personal. It will only alienate her, create friction between you, and ultimately lead to more problems and misbehavior.

Although it may work in the moment, which is why the strategy is so common, your reminder is actually creating, reinforcing, and cementing a limiting belief she has about herself.
Although Brittany may be the only one who pushes other students while jostling to get in line, you remind everyone.
